23142-in-search-of-el-dorado:
Two adventurers trade the sea for the jungle in In Search of El Dorado. Chance threw the two men together and proved their mettle. After that the sea lost them. Swamps and forests of the Amazon Valley claimed them instead, with amazing adventures ahead. Dick Cavendish had shipped as fifth officer of the Everest.

El Dorado, the golden kingdom that swallowed expeditions whole, draws Dick and his companion upriver in Harry Collingwood's credited adventure. Piranha water, lost trails, and hostile country replace the quarterdeck's order. Boys' imperial fiction ran on such substitutions, salt water for black water. The Amazon chapters keep the pace of the sea chapters, with greener dangers and the same stout hearts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-tostad:
Alonso Tostado, or Tostatus, was an exegete, born at Madrigal about 1400, dead near Avila in 1455. After Franciscan grammar school he entered Salamanca, studying philosophy, theology, law, Greek, and Hebrew. By application, brilliance, and a retentive memory, his learning made contemporaries call him the wonder of the world. Aged twenty-two, he lectured on many subjects to large audiences and later assisted with distinction at Basle.

While visiting the papal court at Siena in 1443, Eugene IV received a denunciation of him for heretical propositions, but assured the pontiff of his orthodoxy by letter. In his Defensorium against Torquemada and critics, he opposed the pope's authority. Back in Spain, he rose to Chancellor of Castile, then Bishop of Avila in 1449, source of his title Abulensis. Besides a Spanish Eusebius commentary, he wrote on Old Testament histories to Second Paralipomenon and on Matthew's Gospel. These digressions appeared at Venice in thirteen folio volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonzo-de-alv:
Alonzo de Alvarado, Knight of Santiago, born at Secadura de Trasmiera near Burgos, date unknown, died in 1559. He went to Peru with Pedro de Alvarado in 1534, no relative of the latter. Charged by contemporaries with avarice and cruelty, he was unflinching for Spain through Peru's civil wars from about 1537 to 1555. He always sided with the crown's sincere representatives, not always profitably. In the bloody troubles that followed he served as a prominent leader, always unsuccessful in immediate command.

Still, a mainstay of the Spanish cause, he held high position. When Hernández Girón rebelled in 1553, Alvarado commanded against him, but at Chuquinga in 1554 suffered a signal defeat. Melancholy after that disaster, he wasted away and died five years later. His chief achievement, pacifying Chachapoyas in northeastern Peru in 1535 and 1536, was the first step from Peru towards the Amazon basin. He married in Spain on a short visit in 1544.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mondonedo: Mondoñedo, the Galician cathedral city, has been a bishop's see since the early Middle Ages. This entry covers its diocese, its bishops, and its history. The faith in green Galicia, where the bishops of Mondoñedo ruled for a thousand years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nardo: Nardò, the Baroque town of the Salento, has been a bishop's see since the early Middle Ages. This entry covers its diocese, its churches, and its history. The faith in the heel of Italy: its baroque cathedral dominates the Salentine plain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oviedo: Oviedo is the Asturian capital whose Cámara Santa guards the relics of the Reconquista. This entry covers its archdiocese, its bishops, and its history. The cradle of Christian Spain: its Asturian kings began the centuries-long Christian Reconquista all by itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-de-alva: Pedro de Alvarado was Cortés's fiery lieutenant who conquered Guatemala. This entry covers his campaigns, his cruelty, and his death. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-de-rega: St. Peter Regalado was the Franciscan reformer of 1400s Spain, famed for his ecstasies. This entry traces his life, his reform, and his canonization. The seraph of Valladolid: his wondrous miracles drew the wondering crowds of old Castile to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-lando: Lando was the pope of 913 whose six months left barely a name. This entry notes his brief pontificate and the scant records. The most obscure of all popes: his bare name survives on a dusty papal list all alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhodo: Rhodo was the Christian writer against Marcion. This brief entry notes his fragments, his testimony, and his age. A voice of the second century: his brave pen answered the heretic Marcion in Rome's church of the 100s' fierce debates on Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-odo: St. Odo was the second abbot of Cluny. This entry traces his reform, his music, and his fame. The restorer of the Burgundian abbey: his solemn chant reformed Cluny in the 900s' decades of the abbots of Burgundy's house in France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-arialdo: St. Arialdo was the martyr of the Pataria. This entry traces his Milan, his reform, and his death. The deacon of the Lombard reform: his martyr's blood sealed 1066 in the lake of Como in the waters of the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-odo: St. Odo was the abbot of Cluny. This entry traces his reform, his music, and his fame. The second founder of the Cluniac order: his reformed rule crowned Cluny in the 920s' Burgundy in the east of the duchy in the Grosne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-trudo: St. Trudo was the abbot of the Belgian house. This entry traces his Sint-Truiden, his rule, and his cult. The founder of the Hesbaye abbey: his new rule crowned Sint-Truiden in the 650s' Hesbaye in the town of the Cicindria.
grillparzer-die-judin-von-toledo:
King Alfonso the Eighth of Castile loves Rahel, a Jewish woman of Toledo, and the passion shakes his throne. Grillparzer's Die Juedin von Toledo, given here in German, builds a tragedy from Spanish legend. Desire, power, and prejudice close around the lovers until murder ends the affair.

The court sees a kingdom endangered; the king sees only the woman he wants. Grillparzer refuses easy villains, spreading blame across fear, ambition, and custom. Rahel's death exposes the cruelty that polite society hides under reasons of state. The play ranks among the most powerful historical tragedies of the nineteenth century. Its questions about tolerance and power have not aged at all.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner turns south for this fifth volume of legends. Its contents promise swims, sirens, and sacred fires. The Swim at Indian Head opens near government proving grounds. Great guns now racket where an old Native town once stood.

That town loved fight, and its tales keep a fierce edge. Moaning sisters, a lake of the Dismal Swamp, and Natural Bridge follow. Atlanta's wraith ringer and Natchez's sacred fire close the list. Heat, pride, and old wars haunt these Southern tales. Skinner gives the region its full share of ghosts, from colonial coast to Civil War fields.
on-commando:
Dietlof van Warmelo wrote this memoir of the Boer War. Methuen published it in London in 1902. The contents trace his service with a Boer commando. Early chapters enter Natal and reach Dundee and Ladysmith. He describes the siege and the blowing up of cannon.

Later chapters follow flight from Pretoria and guerrilla life. Van Warmelo rides with Presidents Steyn and Kruger. He gets lost in the bushveld with Steyn. Practical hints and adventures on the Sabie River close the book. The memoir gives a Boer fighter's view of the war. It balances battle, hardship, and narrow escapes.
phaedo:
Plato's Phaedo, in Benjamin Jowett's translation, tells the last day of Socrates. Jowett's introduction explains the frame: months or years later, at Phlius, Phaedo narrates the death to Echecrates and friends. The execution had waited thirty days for the sacred ship's return from Delos, and the disciples spent the time in conversation.

On the final morning the friends gather early, and Xanthippe is sent home with the children. Socrates, newly unchained, remarks that pleasure follows pain, and begins his arguments that the soul is immortal. The dialogue joins philosophy to the most famous death scene in literature.
podcast-tuckercarlson--wq6h2MTpdo:
Comedian Roseanne Barr joins Tucker Carlson to watch her own viral Trump speech. Barr's comeback had made her a hero to a new crowd. Her raw style fills the room from the start.

The pair laugh through clips and trade war stories from show business. Barr recalls bans, firings, and the cost of her views. She frames her speech as truth told without a filter. Carlson treats her as a fellow rebel with scars. The episode is joyful and loose, a victory lap for two figures the old media cast out.
the-boy-mechanic-volume-1-700-things-for:
The Boy Mechanic, Volume I, bills itself as 700 Things for Boys to Do, with 800 pictures that show how. Notes bound with it warn that the plain text form is of small use, since so much rests on the drawings. Readers are sent to the full drawn form for the whole book. Old gift marks in it name Jack Mansfield and Ed, with dates in 1916 and 1938.

The notes sort the projects by kind. Some still draw boys today, such as magic, kites, and boomerangs. Some are now pure past, such as chemical photo work, phonographs, and gear for coal stoves. A third kind shows the loose care of 1913 for health and risk. Those builds use gunpowder, lead, mercury, strong acids, and cyanide salts. The notes urge readers to treat such builds as a view of old ways, not as things to try now.
the-cask-of-amontillado:
The Cask of Amontillado, by Edgar Allan Poe, is narrated by a man who bore a thousand injuries from Fortunato and vowed revenge only when insult was added. He defines his code at once. A wrong is unredressed when retribution overtakes its redresser. It is also unredressed when the avenger fails to make himself felt as such. So the punishment must come with impunity. It must also be recognised.

Fortunato's weak point is his pride in connoisseurship of wine. In wine, unlike his countrymen's adopted enthusiasms, he is sincere. The narrator shares the skill. He bought largely of Italian vintages himself. They meet at dusk in the supreme madness of the carnival. Fortunato wears motley with cap and bells, already deep in drink. The narrator greets him warmly. He brings news of a pipe of what passes for Amontillado. He adds his doubts about it.
the-grand-can-on-of-the-colorado:
John Muir wrote The Grand Canon of the Colorado. It is dated 1902. Muir opens with the modern tourist. The wonders of the earth lie spread out and easy before him. Workers grade roads, bore tunnels, and move hills for him. Even tender folk can ride in comfort now. They cross oceans, deserts, and high mountains.

Muir traces the order in which the great western sights came within reach. First came Yosemite and the Big Trees. They came with the first transcontinental line. Then came Yellowstone and Alaska by the northern roads. Last came the Grand Canon, hardest to reach. A branch of the Santa Fe has now made it the most accessible of all. With this spread of steel through the wilderness, Muir warns, there is loss as well as gain.
what-can-she-do:
E. P. Roe wrote What Can She Do?, issued as volume ten of his works. His preface is blunt: the book was not made to amuse. It was written with an earnest aim that he trusts will show in the tale. A verse-like dedication speaks to girls who refuse to wait for someone else to carry them.

Roe warns that more women now face the world with no skills and no training. Crowded trades make that risk worse each year, he says. He also vows to treat a hidden social evil in plain terms. The novel presses a hard question: how can an untrained woman earn an honest living?
